author: fwyzard
body: #### PR description: This PR partially addresses #52253. Currently every module call copies the job's `ServiceToken` (a `std::shared_ptr`), or locks a `ServiceWeakToken` to it, and release it again: in `Path::runNextWorkerAsync` / `workerFinished`, in the worker tasks, in every `ServiceRegistry::Operate`. All threads of the job therefore update the same atomic reference count, whose cache line bounces between cores and sockets; on large two-socket machines this is a bottleneck for the whole job. This PR makes `ServiceToken` a non-owning handle to the services: a plain pointer, trivially copyable, with no reference counting. The ownership moves to a new `OwningServiceToken`, returned by `ServiceRegistry::createSet`, `createContaining` and `createServicesFromConfig`, and held by the owners of the services: `EventProcessor`, `TestProcessor`, `TestSourceProcessor`, `PythonEventProcessor`, `cmsRun`, `PileUp`, and the standalone tools and tests that create their own service set. `ServiceRegistry::Operate` and `presentToken()` are non-owning. All the asynchronous tasks and callbacks (event paths, workers, transforms, stream and global transitions, EventSetup callbacks, delayed reader) copy the caller's `ServiceToken` instead of a `ServiceWeakToken`. `ServiceWeakToken` remains for objects that can outlive the services, e.g. the `TFile` of `TStorageFactoryFile`; `ServicesManager` derives from `std::enable_shared_from_this` so that `OwningServiceToken(ServiceToken)` and `ServiceWeakToken(ServiceToken)` can share or observe the ownership when needed. The services are now created by `ServiceRegistry` once the `ServicesManager` is owned by a `std::shared_ptr`, instead of in its constructor, so that a service can take an owning or a weak token to its own service set in its constructor. Behaviour changes for code outside the framework: - a `ServiceToken` must not outlive the `OwningServiceToken` that owns the services; it cannot be obtained from a temporary `OwningServiceToken` (compile-time error), and `ServiceWeakToken::lock()` returns an `OwningServiceToken`; - code that creates its own services must keep the result in an `OwningServiceToken` (`edm::ServiceToken token = edm::ServiceRegistry::createSet(...)` does not compile any more); this affects the standalone tools and the unit tests of `CondCore`, `FWStorage`, `HeterogeneousCore`, `PhysicsTools` and `FWCore`, updated here; - `setupSiteLocalConfig()` returns a `SiteLocalConfigOperate` that owns the service it makes available; - the module-facing `doTransformAsync` / `transformAsync_` take a `ServiceToken const&` instead of a `ServiceWeakToken const&`; no module outside `FWCore/Framework` implements them. This replaces the earlier version of this PR, which kept the owning token and added a separate `ServiceRegistry::OperateNonOwning` with tokens passed by reference to the tasks, following the [suggestion](https://github.com/cms-sw/cmssw/pull/52158#issuecomment-6200819862) by @Dr15Jones. Making the non-owning handle the default removes the second `Operate`, the reference-lifetime conventions in the tasks, and the changes to `ESProductResolverTemplate` and `SourceCoordinator`, for the same performance. ##### Measurements HLT menu `/online/collisions/2026/2e34/v1.3/HLT/V2`, run 402360 HLTPhysics data read with `DAQSource` from local FRD files, CPU only, jobs pinned with `taskset` to N cores and both of their SMT siblings (threads = streams = cpus), 2 concurrent lumisections, 3 to 4 repetitions per point, error bars = standard deviation. Throughput from the `ThroughputService` over at least 60 s per job. Scaling with the number of cores on a 2 AMD EPYC 9655 machine (2 96 Zen 5 cores; the container leaves out one core per socket, so a full socket has 95 cores and the full machine 190), cores added in order, `CMSSW_20_1_X_2026-10-16-1000`: the reference, and the previous version of this PR together with #52189 (the two are indistinguishable from the previous version alone, and #52189 is now merged). The dashed line is the reference extrapolated linearly from one full CCD (8 cores), so the L3 sharing within a CCD is not counted as a loss. Raw throughput, and the same scaled to the maximum boost clock of 4.5 GHz to remove the effect of the lower clock with more busy cores: The reference stops scaling at about 64-95 cores (447 ev/s with 190 cores, 3.76 GHz); with this change the throughput keeps growing to the full machine (766 ev/s, 2.97 GHz, +71%), and at a fixed clock it follows the extrapolation from one CCD up to about 80 cores and stays within 11% of it on the full machine. These plots were made with the previous version of the code; they will be redone with this version, but the measurement below shows the same gain. With this version, one job on all the cores of the machine, compared with two concurrent jobs each pinned to one socket (`CMSSW_20_1_X_2026-10-19-1100`, average sigma of 3 repetitions, at the measured clock, with the value at 3.2 GHz in brackets): | machine | one job, all cores: IB this PR | two jobs, one per socket: IB this PR | |---|---|---| | 2 EPYC 9534 (124 cores) | 311.2 2.4 [350] 391.4 4.9 [481], +26% | 435.4 0.4 [528] 436.7 2.6 [531] | | 2 EPYC 9655 (190 cores) | 444.4 2.8 [378] 775.1 8.8 [832], +74% | 761.4 0.1 [759] 842.8 1.3 [893], +11% | | 2 EPYC 9965 (382 cores) | 410 1 [393] 502 16 [508], +22% | 852.7 0.5 [917] 1306.2 1.9 [1703], +53% | On the 9965 this PR improves all results, but the single full-machine job remains far below the two per-socket jobs. This will be addressed separately. #### PR validation: Unit tests of `FWCore/ServiceRegistry` (including new tests of the owning / non-owning / weak token semantics and of tokens taken in a service constructor), `FWCore/Framework` and `FWCore/TestProcessor`. The HLT menu above gives identical path decisions to the IB on 4000 events (16 threads, no prescales), and the benchmark jobs (45 per machine, 3 machines) all completed successfully.
title: Rework the Services ownership to improve scaling to large number of cores
